question: Renowned for its excellence, the Castel Goffredo-Mantua Hosiery District is a key Italian and European textile hub.

In 2025, the Commission initiated an anti-dumping proceeding (Commission Notice C/2025/4120) on imports of polyamide yarns from China, causing great uncertainty for companies in the District that use both imported and local yarns and potentially saddling them with retroactive duties and undermining their competitiveness.

By weakening the Mantuan companies that process polyamide yarns, the Commission’s measure will also have a knock-on effect on local businesses that produce these fabrics. It is vital that protection be afforded to companies across the entire textile supply chain, whether they be involved in spinning or other processing and manufacturing activities.

The nature and duration of these duty measures must be made clear and a balance struck between the cost of raw materials and the price of finished products if the textile sector as a whole is to be competitive. In the light of the above: 1.
Will the Commission speed up the aforementioned anti-dumping procedure and clarify both its timeframe and the nature of its duties as soon as possible?
Is the Commission aware that measures which protect yarns at the expense of finished products could harm the Hosiery District’s competitiveness?
Will the Commission ensure that finished EU products are competitive vis-a-vis imported raw materials, thereby protecting all companies and jobs in the Hosiery District?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.4.2026) The anti-dumping procedure follows the standard time schedule. Since October 2025 imports are registered1, and provisional anti-dumping measures, ranging from 57,7% to 90,1% were imposed on 28 March 20262. Definitive measures, if warranted, will be published by 25 September 2026, at the latest.

The impact of anti-dumping measures on the downstream industries is analysed in the context of EU interest analysis. However, this requires cooperation of the users of polyamide yarns. Upon initiation, 140 users of polyamide yarns identified in the complaint were invited to cooperate. Only three users and one user’s association, registered themselves as interested parties.

None of them filled in the user questionnaire. Only one provided comments concerning the product scope and not on the impact of measures on the downstream industry. Two other users (not registered as interested parties) provided general comments on the possible negative impact of the measures on the downstream industry, but these were not supported by any evidence or data.

The trade defence instruments used by the Commission are designed for restoring the level playing field on the EU market when it is disrupted by unfair practices of dumped imports. Following the imposition of provisional measures, the Commission will further assess the effect of the measures on the EU producers and users of polyamide yarns.
In case the downstream industry faces pressure from cheap imports, it can also submit a complaint and request an anti-dumping investigation.
1 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1984 of 3 October 2025 making imports of yarns of

polyamide originating in the People’s Republic of China subject to registration (OJ L 2025/1984, 6.10.2025: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2025/1984/oj/eng). 2 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/734 of 26 March 2026 imposing a provisional anti-dumping duty on imports of yarns of polyamide originating in the People’s Republic of China (OJ L 2026/734, 27.03.2026: ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2026/734/oj).
